regimes.","hypothesis_id":null}],"hypotheses":[],"feedback_interpretation":"Recent measured outcomes confirmed that the largest generalization risk is local structure-condition curvature. m178, m199, m164, m159, and m92 showed that similar solvent ratios can produce sharply different endpoint responses, while m80 remained compact despite delayed related carbonyl predictions. The nitrogen feedback was especially heterogeneous: pyridyl, nitrile-benzophenone, phosphonium, and amino-aryl rows produced distinct tails, with m66 and m90 providing strong evidence against a single nitrogen correction. Donor-rich measurements such as m119, m120, m205, m206, and m207 also showed long completion tails and amount-sensitive onset. The corrected batch therefore combines matched ratio pairs, strong-solvent anchors, weak-solvent boundary points, ordinary compact controls, and loading contrasts across aromatic acceptors, nitrogen compounds, esters, and fused-ring structures.","batch_rationale":"This batch is designed to improve the retrained model across the Row-distribution by covering both ordinary rows and the high-error delayed-tail regime. Repeated molecules form interpretable local response curves for m4, m31, m116, m182, m192, and m216, while m75, m83, m89, m95, m103, m194, and m193 broaden transfer across ester, nitrogen, fused-ring, and aromatic-acceptor families. Strong-solvent controls such as m24, m29, m65, m126, m140, m143, m187, and m216 help prevent broad corrections from being learned from only delayed examples. High-ratio points with wide predicted intervals target unsupported boundary behavior, and paired loading amounts expose whether endpoint shifts are caused by sample loading or solvent strength. Together these experiments repair observed failure regions while preserving chemical diversity that can improve generalization beyond any single scaffold."}
